title: Throughput assurance: procurement one-pager for enterprise inference
content:
Executive summary:

This one-pager is a procurement-ready briefing for the enterprise buyer evaluating reserved inference capacity. It distills the promise buyers care about into concrete guarantees, margin-safe contractual language, and sales-ready rebuttals. Use this in customer-facing proposals, SOW drafts, and as talking points during procurement negotiations.

Primary buyer personas:
- Platform/Infrastructure architects: care about isolation, predictable p99 latency, and how we guarantee capacity under bursty workloads.
- ML/Model engineering leads: need consistency for model performance, KV-cache residency, and compatibility with quantized model variants.
- Procurement/Finance: want deterministic unit economics, clear uplifts for burst, and termination/exit terms.
- Security/Compliance officers: need network isolation, auditability, and KMS/HSM integration.

Core positioning statements (short):
- Predictable throughput you can budget for: reserved GPU pools with capacity guarantees and transparent unit economics.
- Isolation without compromise: customer-dedicated pools and network segmentation to meet regulatory and tenancy needs.
- Operational SLAs that matter: latency SLOs, availability guarantees, and defined mitigation for degradation.

Technical guarantees we can commit to (baseline proposal):
- Dedicated pool availability: 99.9% monthly uptime for reserved pools, measured by control-plane and serving-plane checks.
- Latency SLO: p99 token generation latency within X model family <= 200ms for sequences <= 512 tokens on provisioned GPUs under steady-state throughput (define model and HW in SOW).
- Throughput assurance: committed throughput (tokens/sec or requests/sec) per contract; we supply baseline throughput profile (e.g., 20 concurrent rps for gptx-20b equiv on a 4-GPU pool) and an agreed burst policy.
- Isolation: tenant-exclusive GPU allocation, encrypted KV cache at rest, VPC peering or private endpoint, audit logs retained for N days.
- Fallback & graceful degradation: automatic routing to a compatible spare pool or a lower-cost variant under capacity pressure with prior notification and rate/time limits.

Procurement-ready contract language snippets (boilerplate drafts for SOW):
- Capacity commitment: "Provider will allocate and maintain a dedicated inference pool of N GPUs configured to the specifications in Appendix A for the duration of the Term. Committed throughput is defined as T (requests/sec) sustained over a 5-minute rolling window."
- Availability measurement: "Availability will be measured as the percentage of minutes in the billing period where the control-plane and at least one serving node accept requests for the customer's pool."
- Remedy: "If Provider fails to meet Availability SLA in any billing month, Provider will (a) offer pro-rated service credits equal to X% of the monthly fee for each 0.1% below the SLA and (b) provide a remediation plan within 10 business days."
- Data isolation: "All model inputs, KV cache segments, and logs for the customer's endpoints will be stored in tenant-dedicated storage and encrypted with keys managed by the customer's KMS (if enabled)."

Pricing/commitment options (playbook):
- 12/36 month reserved term tiers with stepped discounts (12mo, 24mo, 36mo).
- Option A (Committed steady-state): fixed monthly fee for provisioned pool + metered overage at defined rate. Predictable for finance teams.
- Option B (Committed with burst buffer): baseline commitment lower, includes pre-paid burst credits usable in peak months at a higher per-unit cost. Good for seasonal apps.
- Option C (Capacity + manage): Includes dedicated SRE and higher retention logs for regulatory customers. Priced as uplift percentage.

Competitive differentiation (how to beat vendor X/Y):
- Against major cloud managed endpoints: emphasize our inference-optimized runtime and lower per-token costs at scale due to batching, KV caching, and quantization support.
- Against pure self-hosted inference vendors: emphasize unified support, SLAs, and the operational burden we remove (patching, fallback routing, model rollout).
- Against other inference platforms offering "reserved GPUs": call out transparent per-route telemetry, token-level cost breakdowns, and per-model performance tuning (we give concrete perf baselines).

Common procurement objections + rebuttals:
- "We can run this ourselves cheaper." -> "Upfront capex hides ongoing ops and SRE costs; our telemetry shows typical Total Cost of Ownership crossover for teams above X qps — plus we carry SLA risk and an engineered fallback story."
- "What if we need more capacity quickly?" -> "We offer burst capacity options, ramp guarantees (e.g., add N GPUs within 48 hours for emergency ramps), and automatic spillover to cold pools with clear service-level tradeoffs."
- "How do you prove isolation?" -> "We provide tenant-exclusive allocations, periodic attestation reports, KMS-backed encryption, and support for customer-managed audit exports during onboarding."

Sales enablement checklist (for AE/SE pre-procurement call):
- Validate buyer persona and primary constraints: latency vs throughput vs cost vs compliance.
- Capture expected steady-state RPS, peak RPS, model family/config (float/quant), and average seq length.
- Map to one of the pricing tiers and produce a preliminary TCO slide (include overage policy).
- Offer proof-of-concept: short pilot with capped ramp and telemetry dashboard access.
- Provide sample SOW and SLA excerpts within 48 hours of request.

Example procurement timeline (recommended cadence):
1) Discovery (0–2 weeks): capture workload profile, security checklist, and procurement constraints.
2) Pilot (2–6 weeks): limited reserved pool, integration support, and instrumentation.
3) Negotiation (1–3 weeks): finalize SOW, SLA numbers, and termination terms.
4) Ramp & handoff (0–4 weeks): account onboarding, runbooks, SRE rotation.

Open questions / items for product/legal to resolve (for this doc to be 'final'):
- Decide canonical p99 thresholds for the three model tiers we will promise in SOWs and the measurement methodology (do we use synthetic probes + customer telemetry or only production observed?).
- Define default remediation credit scale (current draft uses X% per delta — legal to set absolute numbers).
- Confirm retention window and export format for audit logs for the 'compliance' pricing uplift.
- Technical appendix: agreed default GPU types and example throughput numbers for 8, 16, 32 GPU pools. Need performance table from Serving Runtime team.

Appendix: sample SOW callouts for Appendix A (what to include in tech spec):
- Model family and version, max sequence length, expected tokenization profile.
- GPU type, memory, NVMe config, and network topology.
- KV-cache policy (size, eviction), optional pre-warming.
- Monitoring endpoints and logging exports (prometheus metrics, request traces, audit log S3 location).

Next steps (action items):
- SEs: run three battlecards with typical buyer scenarios and bring real RPS data from pilot customers (owner: Marco; due: 2025-03-07).
- Product: provide perf table and define the three model tiers for SOWs (owner: Elena; due: 2025-03-14).
- Legal: propose final SLA credit table and required indemnities for procurement templates (owner: Ravi; due: 2025-03-10).

Notes to self / working assumptions (keep in doc):
- This is a working draft; allow tailoring per-customer. Do not publish as final until product/legal input received.
- Keep the language modular so we can replace numbers with customer-specific agreed values.
